sections.html:
The Discus was first introduced to aquarists in 1933 and created a sensation. Fully grown, an adult can reach about 6 inches (15 cm) end to end. Viewed from the front Discus are extremely thin for their size, but from the side they are nearly round, hence the name discus, Latin for plate or dish. Their basic body colour in nature is brown. Brilliant blue bars cover both dorsal and anal fins, and extend onto the back and stomach. Dorsal, ventral and anal fins are edged in bright red. A variety from Lake Tefe, Brazil, has bright metallic green or blue bars all over its fins and body and is occasionally called the Royal Discus.

Many varieties (red, yellow, orange, and the yellow-orange Sunset Discus) are not from nature but have been developed through years of careful breeding.

The Discus, like the Angelfish (Pterophyllum) and Cichlasoma festivum, inhabits the huge region known as Amazonas, extending from the middle reaches of the Amazon River far into the jungles of the Venezuelan and Peruvian flood basins.

The Discus is quite commonly found among profuse plant growth in the quiet bends of the rivers, under overhanging banks, and among rock crannies. In shallow areas, it cares for its young beneath the leaves of various Nymphaea species.

The absolute minimum for young Discus is a tank 40 inches (about 100 cm) long, 20 inches (50 cm) wide and 20 inches (50 cm) tall. Adult Discus need a tank 5 feet (about 150 cm) long, or about 75 gallons (about 284 litres) minimum, to be happy and have any chance of breeding successfully. A well planted, well filtered tank is suggested. Discus do not like changes in water conditions, and the larger the body of water, the more gradual the change.

The Discus needs very pure, clean water, filtered through peat, in a well-established planted aquarium. Temperature should be a steady 82°F (28°C), pH 6.5–7.5, 1–12 dGH. For breeding: 86°F (30°C), pH 6–6.5, 0–5 dGH.

The Discus is a finicky eater; it is very important to give a diet of live and frozen food. On a diet of dry flake food they will quickly die, though it may be offered occasionally as a supplement. When rearing fry, the fry feed off the parents' sides, so both male and female need extra protein.

Very peaceful; it does not burrow in the substrate and does not dig up or tear up plants. The Discus lives in harmony with other fish, except at spawning time, when they vigorously defend their young.

It is best to get a group of young Discus and let them pair off; a Discus mates for life. When mates have found each other, they no longer stay with the group but stake out their own part of the aquarium as territory. Only one pair should be left in an aquarium if you want successful breeding. Remove the rest of the young to another aquarium, where another pair may find each other.

Can be sexed only by experts; at spawning time the genital papilla is pointed in males, flat and round in females. When viewed from above at breeding time, females are slightly fatter, due to filling with roe (eggs).

For the first 4 days or so the parents move the fry from place to place in the aquarium, much like angelfish. When the fry become free swimming, they go immediately to the parent's sides and eat something from under the parent's scales, digging their heads under a scale and jerking from side to side. Eventually one parent tires of this and shakes the fry off, and they go to the other parent. This continues for weeks until the young are ready for life on their own among the plants.
